Surah al-Najm (The Star)

Makkan according to al-Hasan, ʿAta', ʿIkrimah and Jabir. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: except for one verse, which is ﴿Those who avoid major sins and indecencies, except for minor faults﴾.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿By the star when it sets﴾, has five opinions:

The first: the stars of the Qur'an when it was revealed, because it was revealed in installments (nujum). This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it refers to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), narrated by Ibn Abi Najih, because they used to fear diseases at its rising.

The third: it refers to Venus (al-Zuhrah), said by al-Suddi, because some of the Arabs used to worship it.

The fourth: it refers to the collective of the stars, said by al-Hasan. It is not impossible to refer to them with the singular form, as ʿUmar ibn Abi Rabiʿah said:

"The most beautiful of the stars in the sky is the Pleiades, and the Pleiades on earth is the adornment of women."

The fifth: it refers to the shooting stars (al-Munqadda). The reason is that when God, exalted is He, intended to send Muhammad (ﷺ) as a Messenger, shooting stars increased before his birth. Most of the Arabs were alarmed by this and went to a blind soothsayer (kahin) of theirs who used to inform them of events. They asked him about it, and he said: "Look at the twelve constellations (buruj). If any of them has been struck by a falling star, it is the end of the world; and if none of them has, then a great matter will happen in the world." They sensed this, and when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, he was the great matter they had sensed. So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾, that is, that star which fell is for this prophethood that has occurred.

In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when it sets﴾ (idha hawa) there are six opinions:

The first: the stars when the devils ascend to them, said by al-Dahhak.

The second: when it falls.

The third: when it sets (ghaba).

The fourth: when it rises.

The fifth: when it descends.

The sixth: when it moves (jara), and its hawy (descent) is its motion, because it never ceases to move in its rising and setting. This is the view of most exegetes.

This is an oath. According to the fifth opinion regarding the shooting of stars, it is a report.

﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ means Muhammad (ﷺ). In it there are two meanings:

One: he did not stray from the aim of truth, nor did he err in following falsehood.

The second: he did not stray by committing error, and he did not err in the sense that his striving failed and he found disappointment, as the poet said:

"Whoever finds good, people praise his affair, and whoever goes astray will not lack blame for his error."

That is: whoever fails in his pursuit, people blame him. This is the answer to the oath according to most scholars. Muqatil said: this is the first surah that the Messenger of God proclaimed openly in Makkah.

﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ has two meanings:

One: he does not speak from his own desire, and he speaks from the command of God. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: he does not speak by desire and lust; rather, it is only a revelation that is revealed, with a command and prohibition from God, exalted is He, to him.

﴿It is only a revelation that is revealed﴾, that is, God reveals it to Jibril, and Jibril reveals it to him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 53, verses 5–18:

﴿He who is mighty in power taught him﴾ refers to Jibril (Gabriel), according to all the scholars.

﴿Possessor of strength, so he stood firm﴾ has five interpretations:

First: possessor of a good appearance; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: possessor of wealth (ghina'); this is the view of al-Hasan.

Third: possessor of strength; this is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah, and from the saying of Khufaf ibn Nadbah:

"I am a man of strength; when calamities befall me, I stand firm (sulayb) against them."

Fourth: possessor of bodily health and freedom from defects; and from the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"I was always among them, one of resource, of firm strength (mihrah), trusted in covenant."

Fifth: possessor of intellect; this is the view of Ibn al-Anbari, who said, the poet said:

"When I met you, I was one of strength; with me is the balance for every disputant."

As for His saying ﴿so he stood firm﴾, it has five interpretations:

First: Jibril stood firm in his place; this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Second: Jibril stood upon his original form in which he was created, for he used to appear to the Prophet in another form, not in the form of a man.

Ibn Mas'ud related that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his true form only twice. As for the first time, he asked him to show himself in his form, and he filled the horizon.

As for the second time, he was with him when he ascended, and this is His saying ﴿and he was on the highest horizon﴾.

Third: the Qur'an stood firm in his chest. On this view there are two possibilities:

One: he became upright in his strength.

Two: in his messengership.

Fourth: it means he rose up. On this view there are two possibilities:

One: it is Jibril who rose to his place.

Two: it is the Prophet ﷺ who rose by the Mi'raj.

﴿and he was on the highest horizon﴾ has two views:

One: it is Jibril, when he saw the Prophet ﷺ on the highest horizon; this is the view of al-Suddi.

Two: it is the Prophet ﷺ who saw Jibril on the highest horizon; this is the view of Ikrimah.

As for "the highest horizon," there are three sayings:

First: it is the rising place of the sun; this is the view of Mujahid.

Second: it is the horizon from which the day comes, meaning the rising of dawn; this is the view of Qatadah.

Third: it is the horizon of the sky, which is one of its sides; this is the view of Ibn Zayd, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"We took the horizons of the sky over you, and for us are its moons, its stars, and its risings."

﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾ has two views:

One: it is Jibril; this is the view of Qatadah.

Two: it is the Lord; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying ﴿came down﴾ has two possibilities:

One: he hung between heaven and earth, for he saw him standing erect and elevated, then he saw him descending; this is the view of Ibn Bahr.

Two: its meaning is "drew near," and from it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and bring [your case] to the rulers﴾, meaning, bring it close to them. The poet said:

"I came to you not presenting a near kinship to you, but I am confident in your generosity."

It has also been said that there is inversion in it, and its sense is: "Then he came down, so he drew near"; this is the view of Ibn al-Anbari.

﴿So he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾ has four views:

First: the measure of two bows; this is the view of Qatadah and al-Hasan.

Second: that it was like the string's distance from the bow; this is the view of Mujahid.

Third: from its grip to its tip; this is the view of 'Abd al-Harith.

Fourth: the measure of two forearms; this is the view of al-Suddi, so "qab" is an expression for the measure, and "qaws" an expression for the forearm.

Then they differed about the meaning of this "near" on three views:

First: that it is Jibril from his Lord; this is the view of Mujahid, and it is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: that it is Muhammad ﷺ from his Lord; this is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Third: that it is Jibril from Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ regarding "His servant" who was revealed to, there are two views:

One: that it is Jibril, peace be upon him, who revealed to him what He revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; this is the saying of 'A'ishah, al-Hasan, and Qatadah.

Two: that it is Muhammad ﷺ to whom it was revealed through the tongue of Jibril; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ regarding "the heart," there are two views:

(p-394) One: he meant the owner of the heart, and he expressed it by "the heart" because it is the pivot of the body and the foundation of life.

Two: he meant the heart itself, because it is the seat of belief. On this there are two views:

One: its meaning is that his heart did not imagine something other than what it is, as one imagines a mirage to be water, so his heart, by imagining the impossible, becomes like one who lies to it. This is the interpretation of those who read ﴿kadhaba﴾ with light stress.

Two: its meaning is that his heart did not deny what his eye saw. This is the interpretation of those who read "kaththaba" with intensification.

Regarding "what he saw," there are five sayings:

First: he saw his Lord with his eyes; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: in a dream; this is the view of al-Suddi.

Third: with his heart. Muhammad ibn Ka'b related, saying: "We said, O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw Him with my heart twice," then he recited ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾.

Fourth: that he saw His majesty; this is the view of al-Hasan. Abu al-'Aliyah related, saying: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked, and he said: 'I saw a river, and beyond the river a veil, and beyond the veil a light; I did not see anything other than that.'"

Fifth: that he saw Jibril in his form twice; this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ has three views:

First: "Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?"; this is the view of Ibrahim.

Second: "Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?"; and this is transmitted (ma'thur).

(p-395) Third: "Will you then cast doubt upon him about what he sees?"; this is the view of Muqatil.

﴿And indeed he saw Him in another descent﴾ means that he saw what he saw a second time after the first. Ka'b said: Indeed Allah, exalted is He, divided His speech and His vision between Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon them both: Muhammad saw Him twice, and Musa spoke with Him twice.

﴿At the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾: two reports have been narrated concerning it.

First: what Talhah ibn Musarrif related from Murrah from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the Prophet ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, which is in the sixth heaven, and to it ends what ascends of the spirits, and from it they are taken; and to it ends what descends from above it, and from it the command is received."

Second: what Ma'mar related from Qatadah from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary was raised for me in the seventh heaven. Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. From its trunk flow two apparent rivers and two hidden rivers. I said: O Jibril, what is this? He said: As for the two hidden rivers, they are in Paradise; and as for the two apparent rivers, they are the Nile and the Euphrates."

Regarding the reason it was named the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, there are five views:

First: because the knowledge of the prophets ends at it, and their knowledge falls short of what is beyond it; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: because deeds end at it and are taken from it; this is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: because the angels and prophets end at it and stop there; this is the view of Ka'b.

Fourth: because everyone who follows the Sunnah and path of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ends at it; this is the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

(p-396) Fifth: because everything that descends from above it and ascends from below it ends at it; this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ has two views:

One: the Garden of abode and dwelling; this is the view of 'Ali and Abu Hurairah.

Two: that it is the abode of the martyrs; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is on the right of the Throne.

Regarding the mention of the Garden of Refuge there are two views, according to what we have mentioned concerning the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary:

One: that the purpose of mentioning it is to identify its location as being near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary; this is the view of the majority.

﴿When there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾ has three sayings:

First: that what covered it was a bed of gold; this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, and he related it as a marfu' report.

Second: that they were the angels; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: that it was the light of the Lord of Glory; this is the view of al-Dahhak.

If it is asked, why was the Lote-tree chosen for this matter rather than other trees? It is said: because the Lote-tree is distinguished by three attributes: far-reaching shade, delicious taste, and fragrant smell. It resembles faith, which combines speech, action, and intention. Its shade is like action, because it extends beyond it; its taste is like intention, because it is hidden within; and its fragrance is like speech, because it is manifest.

﴿The eye did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾: regarding the swerving of the eye there are three views:

First: its deviation.

Second: its departure; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: its diminishing; this is the view of Ibn Bahr.

Regarding its transgression there are three views:

First: its rising above the truth.

Second: its going beyond the truth; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-397) Third: its excess; and the meaning of the statement is that he saw that thing upon its truth and reality, without any deficiency of inability to perceive it, nor any excess of imagining it in his solitude; this is the view of Ibn Bahr.

﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ has three sayings:

First: what covered the Lote-tree of the bed of gold; this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

Second: that he saw Jibril when he had filled the horizon with his wings; this is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

Third: what he saw when his eyes slept and he looked with his heart; this is the view of al-Dahhak.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 53, verses 5–18:

﴿He who is mighty in power taught him﴾ refers to Jibril (Gabriel), according to all the scholars.

﴿Possessor of strength, so he stood firm﴾ has five interpretations:

First: possessor of a good appearance; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: possessor of wealth (ghina'); this is the view of al-Hasan.

Third: possessor of strength; this is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah, and from the saying of Khufaf ibn Nadbah:

"I am a man of strength; when calamities befall me, I stand firm (sulayb) against them."

Fourth: possessor of bodily health and freedom from defects; and from the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"I was always among them, one of resource, of firm strength (mihrah), trusted in covenant."

Fifth: possessor of intellect; this is the view of Ibn al-Anbari, who said, the poet said:

"When I met you, I was one of strength; with me is the balance for every disputant."

As for His saying ﴿so he stood firm﴾, it has five interpretations:

First: Jibril stood firm in his place; this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Second: Jibril stood upon his original form in which he was created, for he used to appear to the Prophet in another form, not in the form of a man.

Ibn Mas'ud related that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his true form only twice. As for the first time, he asked him to show himself in his form, and he filled the horizon.

As for the second time, he was with him when he ascended, and this is His saying ﴿and he was on the highest horizon﴾.

Third: the Qur'an stood firm in his chest. On this view there are two possibilities:

One: he became upright in his strength.

Two: in his messengership.

Fourth: it means he rose up. On this view there are two possibilities:

One: it is Jibril who rose to his place.

Two: it is the Prophet ﷺ who rose by the Mi'raj.

﴿and he was on the highest horizon﴾ has two views:

One: it is Jibril, when he saw the Prophet ﷺ on the highest horizon; this is the view of al-Suddi.

Two: it is the Prophet ﷺ who saw Jibril on the highest horizon; this is the view of Ikrimah.

As for "the highest horizon," there are three sayings:

First: it is the rising place of the sun; this is the view of Mujahid.

Second: it is the horizon from which the day comes, meaning the rising of dawn; this is the view of Qatadah.

Third: it is the horizon of the sky, which is one of its sides; this is the view of Ibn Zayd, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"We took the horizons of the sky over you, and for us are its moons, its stars, and its risings."

﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾ has two views:

One: it is Jibril; this is the view of Qatadah.

Two: it is the Lord; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying ﴿came down﴾ has two possibilities:

One: he hung between heaven and earth, for he saw him standing erect and elevated, then he saw him descending; this is the view of Ibn Bahr.

Two: its meaning is "drew near," and from it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and bring [your case] to the rulers﴾, meaning, bring it close to them. The poet said:

"I came to you not presenting a near kinship to you, but I am confident in your generosity."

It has also been said that there is inversion in it, and its sense is: "Then he came down, so he drew near"; this is the view of Ibn al-Anbari.

﴿So he was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾ has four views:

First: the measure of two bows; this is the view of Qatadah and al-Hasan.

Second: that it was like the string's distance from the bow; this is the view of Mujahid.

Third: from its grip to its tip; this is the view of 'Abd al-Harith.

Fourth: the measure of two forearms; this is the view of al-Suddi, so "qab" is an expression for the measure, and "qaws" an expression for the forearm.

Then they differed about the meaning of this "near" on three views:

First: that it is Jibril from his Lord; this is the view of Mujahid, and it is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: that it is Muhammad ﷺ from his Lord; this is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Third: that it is Jibril from Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ regarding "His servant" who was revealed to, there are two views:

One: that it is Jibril, peace be upon him, who revealed to him what He revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; this is the saying of 'A'ishah, al-Hasan, and Qatadah.

Two: that it is Muhammad ﷺ to whom it was revealed through the tongue of Jibril; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ regarding "the heart," there are two views:

(p-394) One: he meant the owner of the heart, and he expressed it by "the heart" because it is the pivot of the body and the foundation of life.

Two: he meant the heart itself, because it is the seat of belief. On this there are two views:

One: its meaning is that his heart did not imagine something other than what it is, as one imagines a mirage to be water, so his heart, by imagining the impossible, becomes like one who lies to it. This is the interpretation of those who read ﴿kadhaba﴾ with light stress.

Two: its meaning is that his heart did not deny what his eye saw. This is the interpretation of those who read "kaththaba" with intensification.

First: he saw his Lord with his eyes; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: in a dream; this is the view of al-Suddi.

First: "Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?"; this is the view of Ibrahim.

Second: "Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?"; and this is transmitted (ma'thur).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 53, verses 19–26:

﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza?﴾ As for al-Lat, al-A'mash used to pronounce it with a shadda (doubled lam), while the rest of the readers (qurra') read it with a light pronunciation (takhfif). For those who read it lightly, there are two opinions:

The first: it was an idol in al-Ta'if. They claimed that its custodian used to knead sawiq (a porridge of toasted grain) on it for his companions. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: it was a rock on which sawiq was kneaded, between Makkah and al-Ta'if. This was said by Ikrimah.

As for those who read it with a shadda, they also have two opinions:

The first: it was a man who used to knead sawiq on the stone, and no one drank from it without his deity growing fat. When he died, they turned him over onto his grave. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: it was a man who attended to their gods and kneaded sawiq for them at al-Ta'if. This was said by al-Suddi (p-398). It was also said that he was Amir ibn Zirb al-Adwani, and then they took his grave as an idol to be worshipped. A poet said:

"Do not help al-Lat, for surely God will destroy it,
and how can it help you, when it cannot help itself?"

As for "al-Uzza," there are two opinions:

The first: it is an idol they used to worship. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it is a tree on which they hung garments of colored wool (ihn), and which was worshipped by Sulaym, Ghatafan and Jusham. Muqatil said: it is a samurah tree (acacia-type). Al-Kalbi said: it is the one to which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, until he cut it down. Abu Salih said: rather, it was a palm tree on which curtains and wool were hung.

It is also said regarding al-Lat and al-Uzza that there is a third view: they were two houses (shrines) which the polytheists worshipped in the Jahiliyyah. Al-Lat was a house at Nakhlah which the unbelievers of Quraysh worshipped, and al-Uzza was a house at al-Ta'if which the people of Makkah and al-Ta'if worshipped.

﴿And Manat, the third, the other one﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

The first: it was an idol at Qudayd, between Makkah and Madinah. This was said by Abu Salih.

The second: it was a shrine at al-Masllak which the Banu Ka'b worshipped.

The third: they were idols of stone in the Ka'bah which they worshipped.

The fourth: it was an idol at which they shed blood, drawing near to it thereby. For this reason Mina was so named, because of the abundance of blood shed there.

He said "Manat, the third, the other one" because among the polytheists it was ranked in veneration after al-Lat and al-Uzza. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Aliyah al-Riyahi narrated that when this verse was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza..." up to the verse,

Shaytan cast upon his tongue: "Those are the exalted cranes, and indeed their intercession is hoped for." In the narration of Abu al-Aliyah: "and their intercession is approved, and their like is not forgotten." The polytheists rejoiced and said: "He has mentioned our gods." Then Jibril descended and said: "Recite to me what I brought you," and he recited it to him. He said: "I did not bring you this; this is from Shaytan." So God revealed: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he desired, Shaytan cast into his desire﴾ and ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾, where they made the angels daughters of God.

﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

The first: a crooked division. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: an unjust division. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: a deficient division. This was said by Sufyan and most of the lexicographers. A poet said:

"If you turn away from us, we will diminish you, and if you stand, your share is deficient and your nose is humbled."

Here "mad'uz" means deficient.

The fourth: a contrary division. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿Or does man have what he desires?﴾ Concerning this there are two meanings:

The first: of sons, that they should be his exclusively and not daughters.

The second: of prophethood, that it should be in him and not in others.

﴿To God belong the Hereafter and the first (life)﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings:

The first: meaning that He is more capable than His creation; so if it were permissible for Him to have a child—as the polytheists attributed to Him when they made daughters for Him and not sons, exalted is He far above that—then He would be more entitled to sons than they.

The first: it was an idol in al-Ta'if. They claimed that its custodian used to knead sawiq (a porridge of toasted grain) on it for his companions. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: it was a rock on which sawiq was kneaded, between Makkah and al-Ta'if. This was said by Ikrimah.

As for those who read it with a shadda, they also have two opinions:

The first: it was a man who used to knead sawiq on the stone, and no one drank from it without his deity growing fat. When he died, they turned him over onto his grave. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: it was a man who attended to their gods and kneaded sawiq for them at al-Ta'if. This was said by al-Suddi (p-398). It was also said that he was Amir ibn Zirb al-Adwani, and then they took his grave as an idol to be worshipped. A poet said:

"Do not help al-Lat, for surely God will destroy it,

The first: it is an idol they used to worship. This is the view of the majority.

The second: that it is whatever has been forbidden with a prescribed punishment (hadd). This is related by some jurists.

The third: that it is whatever is not expiated except by repentance. This is related by Ibn 'Isa.

One: that they are all sins.

The second: that they are fornication (zina).

The first: "except the lapses they committed in the Jahiliyyah of wrongdoing and immoralities, for these are pardoned in Islam." This was said by Ibn Zayd ibn Thabit.

The second: it is that one approaches them, commits them, and then repents from them. This was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The third: it is that one resolves to have intercourse and then turns away from it, abandoning it. 'Amr ibn Dinar related from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet ﷺ said:

"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much, and which of Your servants has not committed lapses?"

The fourth: that lapses are what is less than intercourse: kissing, touching, a glance, and lying together. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 53, verses 27–32:

﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾. As for "the major sins of wrongdoing" (kaba'ir al-ithm), there are five opinions regarding them.

The first: that it is associating partners with Allah (shirk). This is related by al-Tabari.

The second: that it is whatever has been forbidden with a prescribed punishment (hadd). This is related by some jurists.

The third: that it is whatever is not expiated except by repentance. This is related by Ibn 'Isa.

The fourth: what Shurahbil related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the major sins, and he said: (That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you; that you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you; and that you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife)."

The fifth: what Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated, that a man asked Ibn 'Abbas about the major sins, "Are they seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seven hundred than to seven. There is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence." So it is as if he is mentioning that the major sins are those for which one has not sought forgiveness.

As for "the immoralities" (al-fawahish), there are two opinions:

One: that they are all sins.

The second: that they are fornication (zina).

As for the excepted "minor lapses" (al-lamam), there are eight opinions:

The first: "except the lapses they committed in the Jahiliyyah of wrongdoing and immoralities, for these are pardoned in Islam." This was said by Ibn Zayd ibn Thabit.

The second: it is that one approaches them, commits them, and then repents from them. This was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The third: it is that one resolves to have intercourse and then turns away from it, abandoning it. 'Amr ibn Dinar related from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet ﷺ said:

"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much, and which of Your servants has not committed lapses?"

The fourth: that lapses are what is less than intercourse: kissing, touching, a glance, and lying together. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. Tawus related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I have not seen anything more akin to lamam than the saying of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ: (Allah has written for every soul its share of adultery, which it will surely encounter. The adultery of the eyes is the gaze, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the soul wishes and desires, and the private parts either confirm that or deny it)."

The fifth: that lamam are minor sins.

The sixth: that lamam is what does not incur a prescribed punishment in this world and does not deserve punishment in the Hereafter. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The seventh: that lamam is the first glance; if it is repeated, it is no longer a lamam. This was said by some of the Successors, who thus made it what is not repeated among sins, and he cited the poet's verse:

"He who sees nothing but a passing glance is not equal to one who is inclined to it and does not turn away from it."

The eighth: that lamam is marriage. This is the saying of Abu Hurayrah.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a man called Nabhan the date-seller, who had a shop in which he sold dates. A woman came to him to buy dates, and he said to her: "Inside the shop there is something better than this." When she entered, he solicited her, but she refused and left. Nabhan regretted it and came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, there is nothing a man does except that I have done it, except intercourse." He said: "Perhaps her husband is away fighting (in the cause of Allah)." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth﴾, meaning He produced Adam.

﴿And when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers﴾. Makhul said: "In the wombs of our mothers. Some of us fell [died] and some of us remained. Then we became young boys, and some of us perished and some remained. Then we became youths, and some of us perished and some remained. The second: do not commit sins and say, "We do acts of obedience." This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: when you do good, do not say, "I did such and such."

It may also carry a fourth meaning: do not exchange your ugliness for beauty, or your evil for good.

It may also carry a fifth meaning: do not show off your deeds to the creatures so that they consider you pure.

﴿He knows best who is mindful of Allah﴾. Al-Hasan said: Allah knows every soul, what it is doing, what it is making, and to what it is returning.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 53, verses 33–41:**

﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ There are three opinions about it:

The first: he is al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. This was said by Mujahid. He used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), listen to what they were saying, and then turn away from them.

The third: he is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who gave five young she-camels to a poor man among the Emigrants when he apostatized from his religion, and guaranteed that he would bear the sin of his turning back. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿And gave a little and then withheld﴾. There are four interpretations of it:

The first: he gave a little of himself by enjoying [forbidden pleasures], then he withheld by stopping. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: he obeyed a little and then disobeyed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-403) The third: he gave a little of his wealth and then withheld. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: he gave with his tongue and withheld with his heart. This was said by Muqatil.

Regarding the word *akda* (أكدى), there are two views:

One: it means he cut off (قطع). This was said by al-Akhfash.

The second: it means he withheld (منع). This was said by Qutrub.

﴿Has he knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ There are two interpretations of it:

One: its meaning is: has he been informed of the unseen, so that he sees that what he heard is false?

The second: the Qur'an was revealed to him, so he sees that what he did is true. This was said by al-Kalbi.

It may also bear a third meaning: has he known that there will be no resurrection, so that he sees that there will be no recompense?

﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his commitments]﴾. There are seven opinions about it:

The first: he fulfilled the practice of four rak'ahs at the beginning of each day. This was narrated by al-Haytham from Abu Umama, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second: that he would say, whenever he entered the morning and evening, ﴿So exalted is Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾, and so on, to the end of the verse.

This was narrated by Sahl ibn Mu'adh, from Anas, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The third: [he fulfilled] what he was commanded regarding obedience to his Lord. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: ﴿That no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾, because between Noah and Abraham a man was held responsible for the wrongdoing of his son and his father, and Abraham was the first to oppose them in this. This was said by al-Hudhayl.

The sixth: he did not undertake any command without carrying it out, and did not make any vow without fulfilling it. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan.

The seventh: [he fulfilled] what he was tested with: the slaughter of his son, his being thrown into the fire, and [his people's] denial of him.(p-404)

This is the commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 53, verses 56–62:

﴿This is a warner of the warners of old.﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: Muhammad is a warner of the truth, with which the prophets before him warned. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The second: The Qur'an is a warner with what the earlier scriptures warned. This is the view of Qatadah.

It may also bear a third opinion: that the destruction of the earlier nations mentioned above is a warning to you.

﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near.﴾ That is, the Hour has come near and the Resurrection has approached. It is called "the Imminent" (al-Azifah) because of the nearness of its occurrence in His sight.

﴿There is none to disclose it apart from Allah.﴾ That is, no one can remove its harm.

﴿Do you then marvel at this discourse?﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

One: At the Qur'an, as to its descent from Allah.

The second: At the Resurrection and the recompense, and this is a possibility.

﴿And you laugh and do not weep?⁠﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

One: You laugh in mockery and do not weep in restraint.

The second: You rejoice and do not grieve, and this is a possibility.

﴿While you are sāmidūn?⁠﴾ Regarding this there are nine interpretations:

The first: Proudly (shāmikhūn), as a camel swaggers proudly. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: Heedless (ghāfilūn). This is the view of Qatadah.

The third: Turning away (muʿriḍūn). This is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: Arrogant (mustakbirūn). This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fifth: Playful and frivolous (lāhūn lāʿibūn). This is the view of ʿIkrimah.

The sixth: It means singing (al-ghinā'); when they heard the Qur'an, they would sing. This is the dialect of Himyar. This is the view of Abu ʿUbaydah.

The seventh: That they sit without praying or waiting for prayer. This is the view of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.

The eighth: Standing for the prayer before the imam stands. This is the view of al-Hasan, and concerning it is what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "he went out while the people were waiting for him standing, and he said: 'What is the matter with me that I see you sāmidīn?'"

The ninth: Gloomy/downcast (khāmidūn). This is the view of al-Mubarrad, who said, the poet said:

"The vicissitudes of time struck the women of the family of Harb, who, because of it, fell into a long silent grief (sumūd)."

﴿So prostrate yourselves to Allah and worship.﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

One: That it is the prostration of recitation of the Qur'an. Ibn Masʿud said this, and in it is evidence that there are prostrations in al-Mufassal (the final surahs of the Qur'an).

The second: That it is the obligatory prostration in the prayer.

One: That it is the prostration of recitation of the Qur'an. Ibn Masʿud said this, and in it is evidence that there are prostrations in al-Mufassal (the final surahs of the Qur'an).

The second: That it is the obligatory prostration in the prayer.

This is the commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 53, verses 56–62:

﴿This is a warner of the warners of old.﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: Muhammad is a warner of the truth, with which the prophets before him warned. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The second: The Qur'an is a warner with what the earlier scriptures warned. This is the view of Qatadah.

It may also bear a third opinion: that the destruction of the earlier nations mentioned above is a warning to you.

﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near.﴾ That is, the Hour has come near and the Resurrection has approached. It is called "the Imminent" (al-Azifah) because of the nearness of its occurrence in His sight.

﴿There is none to disclose it apart from Allah.﴾ That is, no one can remove its harm.

﴿Do you then marvel at this discourse?﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

One: At the Qur'an, as to its descent from Allah.

The second: At the Resurrection and the recompense, and this is a possibility.

﴿And you laugh and do not weep?⁠﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

One: You laugh in mockery and do not weep in restraint.

The second: You rejoice and do not grieve, and this is a possibility.

﴿While you are sāmidūn?⁠﴾ Regarding this there are nine interpretations:

The first: Proudly (shāmikhūn), as a camel swaggers proudly. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: Heedless (ghāfilūn). This is the view of Qatadah.

The third: Turning away (muʿriḍūn). This is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: Arrogant (mustakbirūn). This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fifth: Playful and frivolous (lāhūn lāʿibūn). This is the view of ʿIkrimah.

The sixth: It means singing (al-ghinā'); when they heard the Qur'an, they would sing. This is the dialect of Himyar. This is the view of Abu ʿUbaydah.

The seventh: That they sit without praying or waiting for prayer. This is the view of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.

The eighth: Standing for the prayer before the imam stands. This is the view of al-Hasan, and concerning it is what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "he went out while the people were waiting for him standing, and he said: 'What is the matter with me that I see you sāmidīn?'"

The ninth: Gloomy/downcast (khāmidūn). This is the view of al-Mubarrad, who said, the poet said:
